LONDON, England (CNN) -- Scientist and author Stephen Hawking is "very ill" and has been hospitalized, according to Cambridge University, where he is a professor. Stephen Hawking in Pasadena, California, in March. Cambridge University said the 67-year-old is "comfortable" and will stay overnight at Addenbrookes Hospital in Cambridge. Hawking, one of the world's most famous physicists, is also a cosmologist, astronomer, and mathematician. Wheelchair-bound Hawking is perhaps most famous for "A Brief History of Time," which explored the origins of the universe in layman's terms. The book is considered a modern classic. Hawking has Lou Gehrig's Disease (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, or ALS), which is usually fatal after three years. Hawking has survived for more than 40 years since his diagnosis. On his Web site, Hawking has written about living with ALS. "I try to lead as normal a life as possible, and not think about my condition, or regret the things it prevents me from doing, which are not that many," he wrote. He added: "I have been lucky, that my condition has progressed more slowly than is often the case. But it shows that one need not lose hope." The disease has left him paralyzed -- he is able to move only a few fingers on one hand. Hawking is completely dependent on others or technology for virtually everything -- bathing, dressing, eating, even speech. He uses a speech synthesizer with an American accent. Hawking has been married and divorced twice. In 2004, police completed an investigation into accusations by Hawking's daughter that his second wife was abusing him. Authorities said they found no proof. His Web site says he has three children and one grandchild. Hawking was born in Oxford, England, on what turned out to be an auspicious date: January 8, 1942 -- the 300th anniversary of the death of astronomer and physicist Galileo Galilei. A Cambridge University spokesman told CNN: "Professor Hawking is very ill and has been taken by ambulance to Addenbrookes Hospital, Cambridge." Professor Peter Haynes, head of the university's department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics, said: "Professor Hawking is a remarkable colleague, we all hope he will be amongst us again soon." At Cambridge, he holds the position of Lucasian Professor Mathematics -- the prestigious post held from 1669 to 1702 by Sir Isaac Newton. Hawking has guest-starred, as himself, on Star Trek: The Next Generation and The Simpsons. He also said if he had the choice of meeting Newton or Marilyn Monroe, his choice would be Marilyn. In October, CNN's Becky Anderson interviewed Hawking. The following are some quotes from that interview: . "Over the last twenty years, observations have to a large extent confirmed the picture I painted in 'A Brief History of Time.' The one major development that was not anticipated was the discovery that the expansion of the universe is accelerating now, rather than slowing down... We live in the most probable of all possible worlds." CNN's Jennifer Pifer contributed to this report .

# Stephen Hawking hospitalized in Cambridge after becoming ‘very ill’

**CAMBRIDGE, England —** Renowned physicist Stephen Hawking was admitted to a Cambridge hospital Monday after becoming “very ill,” according to the University of Cambridge.

Hawking, then 67, was undergoing tests at Addenbrooke’s Hospital, the university said. He had been unwell for several weeks and had canceled a planned appearance in the United States.

A university spokesperson later said Hawking was comfortable, without providing further details about his condition.

One of the world’s most recognizable scientists, Hawking had spent decades investigating black holes, gravity and the origins of the universe. He held Cambridge’s prestigious Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics, a position once occupied by Isaac Newton, from 1979 until his retirement in 2009.

## A career that changed modern cosmology

Hawking’s most influential work brought together ideas from Einstein’s theory of relativity and quantum mechanics. In the 1970s, he showed that black holes are not entirely black: Quantum effects near their boundaries cause them to emit particles and gradually lose mass.

The phenomenon became known as **Hawking radiation**. It transformed physicists’ understanding of black holes and raised fundamental questions about whether information can be destroyed in the universe.

Hawking also worked with mathematician Roger Penrose on singularity theorems showing that, under broad conditions, Einstein’s equations imply the existence of singularities associated with black holes and the Big Bang.

His 1988 book, **“A Brief History of Time,”** introduced millions of readers to cosmology, black holes and the search for a unified theory of physics. It became an international bestseller and made Hawking a rare scientific celebrity.

## Living for decades with ALS

Hawking was diagnosed at age 21 with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, a progressive neurological disease also known in Britain as motor neurone disease. Doctors initially told him he might have only a few years to live.

Instead, Hawking survived for more than half a century with the condition. As the disease advanced, he lost most voluntary movement and used a wheelchair. After an emergency tracheotomy in 1985 left him unable to speak, he communicated through a computer-based system and speech synthesizer whose electronic voice became internationally familiar.

His unusually long survival made his case medically exceptional, though ALS affected every part of his daily life and required extensive assistance.

## Family and public life

Hawking married Jane Wilde in 1965, and the couple had three children: Robert, Lucy and Timothy. Their marriage ended in divorce in 1995. That year, Hawking married Elaine Mason, one of his former nurses; they divorced in 2006.

His personal life was later depicted in the 2014 film **“The Theory of Everything,”** based on Jane Hawking’s memoir. Eddie Redmayne won an Academy Award for portraying the physicist.

Beyond academic circles, Hawking became a prominent advocate for science and for people with disabilities. He appeared in television programs including “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” “The Simpsons” and “The Big Bang Theory,” often playing a humorous version of himself.

## A lasting scientific legacy

Hawking never received a Nobel Prize, in part because Hawking radiation has not been directly observed from an astronomical black hole. Nevertheless, his ideas remain central to efforts to reconcile gravity with quantum theory.

His work helped turn black holes from obscure mathematical predictions into essential laboratories for testing the deepest laws of nature. It also inspired generations of researchers to examine the relationship among gravity, thermodynamics, information and spacetime.

Hawking died at his Cambridge home on March 14, 2018, at age 76. His ashes were interred in Westminster Abbey, between the graves of Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin.

## Stephen Hawking Hospitalized, Renewing Attention on a Life That Redefined the Universe

**CAMBRIDGE, England —** Stephen Hawking, the British theoretical physicist whose bestselling *A Brief History of Time* brought the mysteries of the universe to a mass audience, was hospitalized in Cambridge in April 2009 after becoming seriously ill with a chest infection.

Cambridge University initially described Hawking, then 67, as “very ill,” prompting concern around the world. He was admitted to Addenbrooke’s Hospital, where his condition later improved and he was reported to be comfortable. Hawking had canceled a planned appearance at Arizona State University because of illness shortly before his hospitalization.

The episode was especially serious because Hawking had lived for decades with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, the progressive motor-neuron disease also known in Britain as motor neurone disease. Respiratory infections can be particularly dangerous for people with the condition.

Yet prolonged survival against daunting medical odds had long been part of Hawking’s extraordinary story.

Diagnosed at 21 while a graduate student at Cambridge, Hawking was initially told he might have only a few years to live. The disease gradually deprived him of movement and speech, but it did not halt his scientific career. He survived for more than half a century after his diagnosis, eventually dying in 2018 at age 76.

“I have lived with the prospect of an early death for the last 49 years,” Hawking told *The Guardian* in 2011. “I’m not afraid of death, but I’m in no hurry to die. I have so much I want to do first.”

### From Oxford to the frontiers of cosmology

Born in Oxford on Jan. 8, 1942—300 years to the day after the death of Galileo Galilei—Hawking studied physics at University College, Oxford, before moving to Cambridge for graduate work in cosmology.

His early research, conducted in part with mathematician Roger Penrose, helped demonstrate that Einstein’s general theory of relativity implied the existence of singularities under broad conditions. The work strengthened the theoretical foundations of the Big Bang model and transformed scientific thinking about the origins of the universe.

Hawking later made his most famous contribution while investigating black holes. In the 1970s, he showed that quantum effects should cause black holes to emit thermal radiation. The phenomenon, now called **Hawking radiation**, overturned the traditional view that nothing could escape a black hole and exposed a deep tension between quantum mechanics, gravity and thermodynamics.

That discovery also helped create the black-hole information paradox: if black holes evaporate, what happens to the information contained in the matter that fell into them? The question remains central to efforts to develop a quantum theory of gravity.

### The Lucasian professor

In 1979, Hawking was appointed Cambridge University’s **Lucasian Professor of Mathematics**, one of the world’s most prestigious academic posts. Established in the 17th century, the chair had previously been held by Isaac Newton and later by Paul Dirac, among other distinguished scientists.

Hawking held the professorship until 2009, when he reached the university’s mandatory retirement age for the position. His tenure cemented his standing not merely as a symbol of perseverance, but as one of the most influential gravitational theorists of his generation.

His physical condition required extensive support. After a severe bout of pneumonia in 1985, Hawking underwent a tracheotomy and lost his remaining ability to speak. He thereafter communicated through a computer system and speech synthesizer, producing the electronic voice that became internationally recognizable.

### A bestseller about the universe

Hawking became a global celebrity with the publication of *A Brief History of Time* in 1988. Written for general readers, the book explored the Big Bang, black holes, the nature of time and the search for a unified theory of physics.

Its commercial success was remarkable for a work of popular cosmology. The book spent years on bestseller lists, sold millions of copies and was translated into dozens of languages. It also became famous for being widely purchased even if not always finished—a reputation Hawking treated with characteristic humor.

The book concluded with one of his best-known lines. If humanity discovered a complete theory of the universe, he wrote, “then we should know the mind of God.” Hawking used “God” largely as a metaphor for the ultimate laws of nature; in later years he spoke more explicitly of his atheism and argued that the universe did not require a divine creator.

His broader public message was often one of curiosity and persistence. In a widely quoted address, he urged people: “Remember to look up at the stars and not down at your feet. Try to make sense of what you see and wonder about what makes the universe exist. Be curious.”

He paired that cosmic perspective with advice grounded in his own experience: “However difficult life may seem, there is always something you can do and succeed at. It matters that you don’t just give up.”

### Scientist and cultural figure

Hawking’s fame extended far beyond academic physics. He appeared as himself on television programs including *Star Trek: The Next Generation*, *The Simpsons* and *The Big Bang Theory*. His life was portrayed in the 2014 film *The Theory of Everything*, with Eddie Redmayne winning an Academy Award for his performance as Hawking.

That celebrity sometimes threatened to overshadow the complexity of his scientific work. But colleagues emphasized that Hawking’s reputation rested first on fundamental contributions to cosmology and black-hole physics. His disability shaped the circumstances under which he worked, but it did not define the substance of that work.

The 2009 hospitalization underscored both his medical vulnerability and the exceptional duration of his life with ALS. What doctors had once expected to be a short illness became a decades-long career in which Hawking repeatedly pushed beyond physical and intellectual boundaries.

His life, he suggested, was evidence that limitation need not extinguish purpose. “Where there’s life,” he once said, “there’s hope.”
